part.text: {"proposals":[{"title":"Speculative multiple-timestep molecular dynamics for protein systems","field":"computational biophysics","sequential_part":"The Verlet time integrator advances one step at a time; slow force evaluations and neighbor-list rebuilds create a step-to-step serial barrier despite parallel force kernels.","restructure":"Run fast bonded/nonbonded substeps concurrently with one speculative slow force evaluation using extrapolated positions; commit substeps and roll back only when a rare collision or large-force rejection triggers a resimulation.","condition":"Slow and fast forces are separable and the speculative rejection rate stays low (roughly below 5%), so rollback recomputation costs less than serial slow-force steps.","baselines":"Reference 2 fs Verlet integration in OpenMM or AMBER on one GPU, comparing timings and energy drift for physical equivalence.","first_test":"Time 1 ns of DHFR, about 23k atoms, with a 4 fs slow / 1 fs fast split against baseline on one GPU; roughly 15-30 min, reporting steps/sec, rollback rate, and energy drift."},{"title":"Parallel-in-time adjoint data assimilation for storm-scale weather","field":"climate science and numerical weather prediction","sequential_part":"4D-Var requires integrating the forecast forward and the adjoint backward through the entire assimilation window one timestep at a time, with the adjoint path itself serially dependent.","restructure":"Use ParaExp/PFASST-style parallel-in-time splitting: a coarse propagator provides initial values so fine timestep chunks integrate concurrently on multiple GPUs, and corrections iterate only where coarse error is large.","condition":"The coarse model is accurate enough that parallel-in-time iterations converge in few passes, and enough GPU memory holds multiple time slices simultaneously.","baselines":"Serial 4D-Var or ensemble Kalman smoother on the same test case, comparing wall-clock, convergence, and analysis RMSE.","first_test":"Lorenz-96 with 40 variables and a 100-timestep window: compare wall-clock and analysis error between serial adjoint and parallel-in-time; roughly $0.05 GPU-hour."},{"title":"Speculative branching for de Bruijn graph genome assembly","field":"genomics and computational biology","sequential_part":"Contig extension walks the assembly graph one supported edge at a time, and the choice at each branch depends on previously committed sequence.","restructure":"Peel the de Bruijn graph in parallel across independent components, and speculatively extend multiple branches at each fork; commit the branch with best read-depth and mismatch support, rolling back rejected alternatives.","condition":"Sequencing coverage is high, such as above 30x, and repeat-induced branches are short enough that speculative alternatives can be enumerated cheaply and resolved by read evidence.","baselines":"SPAdes or Flye contigs or unitigs on the same reads, measured by wall-clock, N50, and sequence identity.","first_test":"Assemble 5 Mb E. coli reads at 100x coverage with speculative branch depth two versus baseline; about 20 min on one GPU, comparing N50, contig length, and runtime."},{"title":"Parallel friends-of-friends halo finding via GPU union-find","field":"astrophysics and cosmology","sequential_part":"Friends-of-friends groups are found by propagating labels through chains of linked particles; on dense filaments that propagation can become a long serial cascade.","restructure":"Replace label propagation with union-find plus pointer jumping and tree contraction: GPU blocks merge edges in parallel, then resolve parent chains via atomic compare-and-swap until roots stabilize.","condition":"Group chains and GPU atomics are handled efficiently in high-bandwidth memory, and approximate grouping order is sufficient for scientific halo catalogs.","baselines":"Serial FoF and/or ROCKSTAR on the same dark-matter particle box, comparing halo mass function and positions.","first_test":"Run group finding on a 10^7-particle test box and compare halo counts and masses to baseline; under about 1 GPU-hour."},{"title":"Reducing the serial contraction path in iterative coupled-cluster amplitude equations","field":"quantum chemistry","sequential_part":"Coupled-cluster amplitude updates have many tensor contractions whose naive order forms a long serial dependence chain, so each iteration is limited by critical path latency.","restructure":"Use algebraic tensor factorization and persistent kernels to flatten the contraction DAG; distribute occupied and virtual blocks across GPUs and overlap communication with compute to shorten the critical path.","condition":"Factorized intermediates preserve numerical accuracy to within convergence tolerance, and interconnect latency is small relative to contracted tensor sizes.","baselines":"PySCF or NWChem CCSD iteration on CPU and single GPU, checked by energy and amplitude convergence.","first_test":"Time one CCSD iteration for a water cluster with cc-pVDZ on 4 GPUs versus single GPU; about 30 min and a few GPU-hours at most."}]}
